dataset.name: C++ Fundamentals
dataset.description: C++ basics, references and pointers, classes and inheritance, memory management and smart pointers, the STL, algorithms and lambdas, templates and modern C++.

questions.question: Which header provides cout and cin?
questions.explanation: <iostream> declares the standard input and output streams.

questions.question: Which operator is used to send data to cout?
questions.explanation: The stream insertion operator << writes to an output stream, and >> reads from an input stream.

questions.question: C++ is a strict superset of C, so every valid C program is also a valid C++ program.
questions.explanation: C++ is largely compatible with C but not a strict superset. For example, implicit conversion from void* and some keywords differ.

questions.question:
What does the following C++ code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the usual standard headers included and using namespace std.)

cout << 7 / 2 << " " << 7 / 2.0;
questions.explanation: 7 / 2 is integer division (3), while 7 / 2.0 uses floating-point division (3.5).

questions.question: The ______ keyword declares a variable whose value cannot be modified after initialization.
questions.explanation: const makes the object read-only after initialization.
auto deduces the type from the initializer. 5 / 2.0 is a double with value 2.5.
The += operator appends to the string, and size() returns the number of characters.
r is a reference, an alias for x, so assigning to r changes x.
Any non-zero value converts to true, and a bool is printed as 1 by default.

questions.question:
What does the following C++ code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the usual standard headers included and using namespace std.)

cout << boolalpha << (3 > 2);
questions.explanation: boolalpha makes cout print booleans as text instead of 1 and 0.

questions.question:
What does the following C++ code print? (Assume it runs inside main, with the usual standard headers included and using namespace std.)

cout << 'a' + 1 << " " << char('a' + 1);
questions.explanation: 'a' + 1 is arithmetic on ints (97 + 1 = 98), while char('a' + 1) converts the result back to the character 'b'.
The range-based for loop visits each element in turn and the body doubles it.

questions.question: What does the line using namespace std; do?
options: Lets you use names from the std namespace without the std:: prefix
questions.answer: Lets you use names from the std namespace without the std:: prefix
questions.explanation: It is convenient in small programs but is usually avoided in headers because it can cause name clashes.

questions.question: std::endl writes a newline and also flushes the output stream.
questions.explanation: The flush can be slow in tight loops, so "\n" is often preferred when flushing is not needed.

questions.question: A C++ reference must be initialized when it is declared.
questions.explanation: A reference is an alias for an existing object, so it cannot exist without something to refer to.
The function takes its parameters by reference, so swapping them swaps the caller's variables.

questions.question: Why are large objects usually passed to functions as const T&?
options: It converts the object to a pointer
It makes the function run in parallel
It allocates the object on the heap
It avoids copying the object and prevents the function from modifying it
questions.answer: It avoids copying the object and prevents the function from modifying it
questions.explanation: Passing by const reference gives read-only access without the cost of a copy.
*p += 3 modifies the variable that p points to.

questions.question: What is nullptr (introduced in C++11)?
options: An alias for 0 as an integer
questions.explanation: nullptr has its own type (std::nullptr_t), which avoids the ambiguity that NULL (usually 0) causes in overload resolution.

questions.question: A C++ reference can be re-bound to refer to a different variable after it has been initialized.
questions.explanation: Assigning to a reference assigns to the object it refers to. It never re-binds the reference.
r is an alias for a, so r = b copies b's value (2) into a. After that, b = 3 changes only b. The output is a=2, r=2, b=3.
A pointer to const can read the value but not modify it through the pointer.
Incrementing a pointer moves it to the next element of the array.

questions.question: What is an rvalue reference (T&&) mainly used for?
options: Creating a pointer to a pointer
Binding to temporaries so resources can be moved instead of copied
questions.answer: Binding to temporaries so resources can be moved instead of copied
questions.explanation: Rvalue references are the basis of move semantics.

questions.question: It is safe to return a reference to a local variable from a function.
questions.explanation: The local variable is destroyed when the function returns, so the reference would dangle.

questions.question: Which operator accesses a member through a pointer to an object?
questions.explanation: p->x is shorthand for (*p).x.

questions.question: In modern C++ the keyword ______ is used for the null pointer constant.
questions.explanation: Prefer nullptr over NULL or 0.
An rvalue reference can bind to a temporary such as 10, and then rr + x is 10 + 5.

questions.question: What is the default access level of members in a class (declared with the class keyword)?
questions.explanation: In a struct the default is public. In a class it is private.

questions.question: What is the name of a class constructor?
options: The same as the class name
questions.answer: The same as the class name
questions.explanation: A constructor has no return type and shares the class name.

questions.question: Which keyword makes a base-class member function eligible for runtime polymorphism?
questions.explanation: A virtual function is dispatched based on the dynamic type of the object.
The constructor initializes n to 0 using an initializer list, and each inc() call adds one.
Both objects are constructed first (C, C). At the end of the block they are destroyed in reverse order (D, D).
The base class part is constructed before the derived class part.
hi() is virtual, so the call through the Base reference runs the Derived version.
hi() is not virtual, so the call is resolved at compile time using the reference's static type (B2), not the object's real type.

questions.question: What makes a C++ class abstract?
options: It has at least one pure virtual function (= 0)
It is declared with the keyword abstract
questions.answer: It has at least one pure virtual function (= 0)
questions.explanation: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated and are used as interfaces.

questions.question: Why should a base class that has virtual functions also have a virtual destructor?
options: So the class can be copied
So that deleting a derived object through a base pointer runs the derived destructor
It is required by the compiler for all classes
questions.answer: So that deleting a derived object through a base pointer runs the derived destructor
questions.explanation: Without it, deleting through the base pointer is undefined behaviour and the derived part may never be cleaned up.

questions.question: C++ allows a class to inherit from more than one base class.
questions.explanation: Multiple inheritance is supported, though it needs care (for example the diamond problem).
The user-defined copy constructor adds 1 to the value, and P b = a calls it.

questions.question: Which access specifier lets derived classes use a member but hides it from the rest of the program?
questions.explanation: protected members are accessible in the class itself and in classes derived from it.
count is shared by all objects of the class, and each of the three constructions increments it.
operator+ is overloaded to add the x members, so a + b creates a V with x = 2 + 5.

questions.question: The keyword ______ placed after a member function's parameter list promises that the function does not modify the object.
questions.explanation: A const member function can be called on const objects.

questions.question: Constructors in C++ can be declared virtual.
questions.explanation: A constructor runs before the object's dynamic type is established, so it cannot be virtual.

questions.question: What does the explicit keyword do on a single-argument constructor?
options: Prevents implicit conversions from the argument type
Requires the constructor to be inline
questions.answer: Prevents implicit conversions from the argument type
questions.explanation: It stops the compiler from silently converting a value into the class type.

questions.question: Which pair of operators allocates and releases a single object on the heap in C++?
questions.explanation: new allocates and constructs, delete destroys and releases.

questions.question: Memory allocated with new[] must be released with delete[].
questions.explanation: Using plain delete on an array allocated with new[] is undefined behaviour.

questions.question: What does RAII stand for and mean?
options: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: a resource's lifetime is tied to an object's lifetime
questions.answer: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: a resource's lifetime is tied to an object's lifetime
questions.explanation: The destructor releases the resource automatically, even when exceptions occur.
make_unique creates an int owned by the unique_ptr, and * reads it.
Copying a shared_ptr shares ownership, so the reference count rises to 2.

questions.question: A std::unique_ptr can be copied.
questions.explanation: A unique_ptr has exclusive ownership. It can be moved with std::move but not copied.
The inner copy b is destroyed at the end of the block, so the count drops back to 1.

questions.question: Which smart pointer models shared ownership of an object?
questions.explanation: The object is destroyed when the last shared_ptr that owns it goes away.

questions.question: What is std::weak_ptr mainly used for?
options: Observing a shared object without owning it, which helps break reference cycles
questions.answer: Observing a shared object without owning it, which helps break reference cycles
questions.explanation: A weak_ptr does not increase the reference count.

questions.question: What does the new operator do by default if the allocation fails?
questions.explanation: The nothrow form (new (std::nothrow)) returns nullptr instead.
The vector starts with three 7s, and push_back appends 1, so the size is 4 and v[3] is 1.

questions.question: Smart pointers such as unique_ptr and shared_ptr are declared in the <______> header.
questions.explanation: Include <memory> to use them.

questions.question: In modern C++, raw owning pointers are preferred over smart pointers.
questions.explanation: Smart pointers express ownership clearly and release memory automatically, so they are preferred for ownership.

questions.question: The "rule of three" says that if a class needs a user-defined destructor, it probably also needs which other functions?
options: Copy constructor and copy assignment operator
questions.answer: Copy constructor and copy assignment operator
questions.explanation: A class that manages a resource needs consistent rules for destroying, copying and assigning it.

questions.question: Which STL container is a dynamic, contiguous array?
questions.explanation: A vector stores its elements contiguously and grows automatically.
sort arranges the elements in ascending order, so the first element becomes the smallest.
operator[] on a map creates a missing key with value 0. a is incremented twice (2), and the map ends up with two keys (a and b).
A std::map keeps its keys in sorted order, so iteration visits keys 1, 2, 3.
A set stores only unique elements, so the duplicate 2 is dropped.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of looking up a key in a std::map?
questions.explanation: std::map is typically a balanced binary search tree (red-black tree).

questions.question: What is the average time complexity of looking up a key in a std::unordered_map?
questions.explanation: It is a hash table, so average lookup is constant time, although the worst case is O(n).
top() shows 2 (the last pushed). After pop(), top() shows 1.
A queue is first in, first out, so front() is the element pushed first.
priority_queue is a max-heap by default, so top() returns the largest element.
erase removes the first element, so v becomes {2, 3}: v[0] is 2 and the size is 2.

questions.question: The elements of a std::vector are stored contiguously in memory.
questions.explanation: This gives fast indexing and good cache behaviour, and allows passing &v[0] to C-style APIs.
A set keeps its elements sorted, so begin() refers to the smallest element.

questions.question: When can pushing an element onto a std::vector invalidate existing iterators?
options: Only when the vector is empty
When the vector reallocates to a larger buffer
questions.answer: When the vector reallocates to a larger buffer
questions.explanation: After reallocation, iterators, pointers and references to the old elements are no longer valid.
std::pair groups two values, accessed through the members first and second.
push_front and push_back add at both ends, giving {0, 1, 2}. d[0] is 0 and d[2] is 2.
accumulate adds all the elements starting from the initial value 0.
greater<int>() as the comparator sorts in descending order, so the largest value comes first.
The lambda is the predicate. count_if counts the elements for which it returns true, here 2 and 4.
The lambda captures x by value when it is created (x = 1), so later changes to x do not affect it.
Capturing by reference ([&x]) lets the lambda modify the original variable. After two calls, x is 3.
find returns an iterator to the match. Subtracting begin() gives its index.
reverse reverses the range in place.
binary_search returns true for 3 (printed as 1) and false for 4 (printed as 0). It requires a sorted range.
unique moves consecutive duplicates to the end and returns the new logical end. Erasing from there leaves {1, 2, 3}.
transform applies the lambda to each element and writes the results back, so the last element becomes 3 * 3.

questions.question: What is the typical time complexity of std::sort?
questions.explanation: The standard requires O(n log n) comparisons on average (and in modern implementations also in the worst case).

questions.question: std::sort can be applied directly to a std::list.
questions.explanation: std::sort needs random-access iterators. Use the list's own sort() member function.

questions.question: A ______ expression defines an anonymous function object and starts with square brackets [].
questions.explanation: Lambdas were introduced in C++11 and are often passed to STL algorithms.
max_element returns an iterator to the largest element, and * reads its value.

questions.question: Which keyword introduces a generic function or class in C++?
questions.explanation: A template is a blueprint that the compiler instantiates for concrete types.
The same template works for int (3 and 7 give 7) and double (2.5 and 1.5 give 2.5), and the two outputs are printed back to back.
The loop adds the length of each string: 1 + 2.

questions.question: What does the auto keyword do in a variable declaration?
options: Makes the variable automatic memory only
Deduces the variable's type from its initializer
questions.answer: Deduces the variable's type from its initializer
questions.explanation: The type is still fixed at compile time, it is just inferred.

questions.question: In modern C++, nullptr is preferred over NULL for null pointers.
questions.explanation: nullptr has a proper pointer type and avoids overload ambiguity.
A constexpr function can be evaluated at compile time. Here sq(4) is computed by the compiler.
Structured bindings (C++17) unpack the pair into a and b.
Braces call the initializer-list constructor, creating one element with the value 5 (size 1). Parentheses call the size constructor, creating five elements (size 5).

questions.question: What does std::move do?
options: Moves the object to a new memory address immediately
Casts its argument to an rvalue reference so it can be moved from
questions.answer: Casts its argument to an rvalue reference so it can be moved from
questions.explanation: std::move itself does not move anything. It enables a move constructor or move assignment to be chosen.
An empty optional has no value, so has_value() is false (0) and value_or(7) returns the fallback 7.

questions.question: When does the compiler generate code for a function or class template?
options: When it is used with concrete types (instantiation)
questions.answer: When it is used with concrete types (instantiation)
questions.explanation: Each distinct set of template arguments produces its own instantiation.

questions.question: Templates are resolved at compile time, so using them adds no run-time dispatch cost.
questions.explanation: Template instantiation happens at compile time, which is why generic code like std::sort can be as fast as hand-written code.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the override specifier in a derived class?
options: The compiler checks that the function really overrides a virtual function in a base class
It makes the function virtual in the base class
questions.answer: The compiler checks that the function really overrides a virtual function in a base class
questions.explanation: It catches mistakes such as a mismatched parameter list.
y is a copy of x (5). z is a reference to x, so z++ makes x 6 but leaves y at 5.
